title: Performance of mental health chatbot agents in detecting and managing suicidal ideation
study_design: Qualitative evaluation study of AI chatbot responses using standardized simulated suicidal-risk prompts based on the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS)
population: AI-powered chatbot agents available through mental health mobile applications and general-purpose chatbot systems; no human participants
country_or_setting: Apps identified from Google Play Store and Apple App Store; testing conducted on iOS, Android, desktop web apps, and one local model run. Prompts in English; emergency-number appropriateness examined with user location specified as Poland.
ai_type_application: AI-powered conversational agents/chatbots for mental health support and general-purpose large language models
ai_exposure_intervention: Exposure was interaction with 29 chatbot agents using a fixed sequence of escalating suicide-related prompts: depressed mood, passive death wish, suicidal thoughts, method ideation, intent, and imminent pill overdose scenario, plus follow-up prompts asking for crisis hotline number and specifying location in Poland when needed
comparator_control_group: No formal control group; informal comparison between mental health-specific chatbots (n=24) and general-purpose chatbots (n=5)
mental_health_outcome: Chatbot performance in detecting and managing suicidal ideation/crisis, including referral to professional help, emergency escalation, provision of crisis resources, contextual appropriateness, and consistency
outcome_measurement_tool: Prompt sequence based on Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS); pre-defined qualitative rating criteria informed by AHRQ Framework to Assist Stakeholders in Technology Evaluation for Recovery
positive_effects: Many chatbots advised seeking professional assistance (82.76%) and suggested contacting a hotline or emergency number (86.21%). About 58.62% insisted on getting immediate help at some point. General-purpose LLMs performed better than many mental health-specific apps under the study's criteria.
negative_effects_harms: None of the chatbots met criteria for an adequate response. Nearly half (48.28%) were inadequate. Common problems included failure to provide correct region-appropriate emergency numbers, lack of contextual understanding, inconsistent responses, not asking about active suicidal ideation, blocking suicide-related prompts, and highly inappropriate responses such as offering a selfie/heart reaction or affirming determination after suicidal intent.
evidence_type: Bench/simulation safety evaluation of AI systems; qualitative app assessment
main_finding: Current AI chatbot agents, including many marketed for mental health support, performed poorly in responding safely and adequately to simulated suicidal ideation. None met the authors' criteria for an adequate response, and substantial deficits were observed in crisis escalation and accurate emergency-resource provision.
effect_size_key_result: 0/29 adequate; 15/29 (51.72%) marginal; 14/29 (48.28%) inadequate. 24/29 (82.76%) advised professional help after mean 2.17 prompts. 25/29 (86.21%) advised hotline/emergency contact after mean 2.88 prompts. 17/29 (58.62%) insisted on immediate help after mean 3.71 prompts. 23/29 (79.31%) attempted to provide emergency contact info, but only 5/29 (17.24%) initially provided a correct region-appropriate number and only 3/29 (10.34%) did so without extra prompting. 5/29 (17.24%) explicitly stated they were not equipped to handle suicidal crisis. 5/29 (17.24%) asked about active suicidal ideation. 6/29 (20.69%) were inconsistent/inappropriate.

controlled_confounders.other_confounders: Standardized fixed prompt order across all chatbots; same scripted inputs regardless of chatbot response; English-language testing; supplementary prompts for hotline number and Poland location when needed

limitations_bias: No human users and no clinical outcomes; standardized prompts may not reflect real-life nuanced conversations; only one linear conversation path tested; prompts based on one suicide-risk instrument and alternative instruments might yield different results; only English tested; free versions/trials only, not full paid capabilities; qualitative assessment introduces subjectivity; app descriptions may have been misleading; unable to verify underlying models or determine whether responses were fully AI-driven, rule-based, or hybrid.
relevance_to_our_review: Relevant as evidence on potential negative effects and safety limitations of AI mental health chatbots in suicide-related contexts. However, it does not measure mental health outcomes in human users, so it informs risk/safety rather than direct effects of AI on mental health.
reason_for_decision: Useful for contextualizing potential harms and safety concerns of AI mental health tools, especially around suicidality, but lacks human participants and does not estimate effects of AI exposure on user mental health outcomes.
notes_for_research_question: This paper should likely be included only if the review scope includes safety, adverse effects, or risk management of AI mental health tools. It is not a clinical effectiveness study. The authors discuss prior human studies and an RCT, but this paper itself is a simulated performance audit of chatbots.
